Hi, everyone. Welcome here today. I'm very excited to be conducting this Q&A with none other than Martin Rocco. Martin is a highly accomplished, well respected, blue ball to yellow ball specialist. Martin has presented in many conferences and his work and passion for developing players is just so inspiring. Martin's work will be of no surprise to many of us who followed his journey on social media and today we're going to explore the pathway to the yellow ball. Martin, how are you this morning? I'm really good. I'm really good. I'm happy to be here. Fantastic. Look, we're very excited to be talking to you. What I really love about Martin's presentation is there's many practical on court examples to go away and test drive coaches, so sit back and enjoy this ride. Martin, my biggest takeaway from your presentation was your lack of ego and your sheer love for coaching players. You see them as people and you're not concerned about them becoming stars, but instead you want to develop people and you want to get them to play tennis for life. How did you shape your philosophy and just tell us a little bit about your journey? Well, first idea is that if we want to create players or we want to create successful players, this is difficult sport. Number one, we have to engage people to get to know the sport, get to know how to play the sport correctly, understand it and try to engage them for a lifetime.

This is a sport that we enjoy every day because tennis is different than other sports that you can play only a few years or until you're 25 or then it's becoming difficult to play because of injuries or lifestyle is different. We have to engage them to play and my idea is to make them the path just as they begin to play, make it very easy. Yeah, no, and that comes across in spades in your presentation. Just along those lines, you mentioned the mistake of introducing too much technique too early in a player's development. Explain again why this can have a detrimental effect on a young players and why do coaches tend to fall into this trap? Well, basically, if we think about the old school, let's say years ago, kids are starting playing tennis when probably they were eight or 10 when you dominate your body much better. Now kids are coming, three, four, five year olds, they're joining the tennis program and what happens is that society already also changed. Kids were much more able to do more stuff in terms of matricity. Now they don't do that. They don't, they play with iPads instead of playing with a bike outside. So what happens that they have less coordination? We have to work on that. If we focus too much on technique with kids that are not that skillful, what happens? We are starting from the very beginning with a very static and I would say boring process. So we have to make them understand how to play the game and start little by little by introducing certain techniques but just guide them to what we want them to reach.

So my idea is to introduce them to the sport and make them understand how to move their body, how to use the throwing ball, getting to know how to use an implement like a racket, moving around the court because tennis is not, I always say this, but tennis is not golf. The ball is not in a steady position. The ball is moving. It's coming from other side, different effects, different directions. So we have to teach the kid how to move around the court. Yeah, and you really seem to teach straight away what's representative of a game. IE you talk about target, reception, projection, variety and teamwork was a big theme of what your presentation was about. Yeah, I think you always talk about tennis being a selfish sport because you play individually all the time. But the thing is, we train collectively. We train groups. We don't have four year olds taking private lessons for 10 years in order to know how to play this sport. So we have which we are coaching in groups. So let's do this. Let's make him play as a team. Be doing cooperation or work that will be make the sessions more dynamic, all the kids will be working together that will be trying to reach certain goals, probably with different capacities, some of the kids will be making some some things much easier than others, but you guide them to what you want them to reach. So my idea is to teach, not thinking about the more skillful kids, trying to get all the kids involved in every activity.

Yeah, and I think some coaches listening in or watching could really resonate with that with team activities. From what I can see, you seem to have a knack in the pedagogical knowledge to give players what they need at exactly the right time and stage in their development. Has this come about from experience? Or did you have some really good mentors? I was from the experience and I've been lucky enough to travel a lot. I worked in Argentina. I'm from Argentina, so I worked in Buenos Aires for nearly 10 years. Then I lived in New York for five years. I've been in Spain for nearly two decades. So what happens is that I've been seeing different ways of teaching different societies, different targets for the kids, different ways you have to communicate. And obviously, when I consider myself like a sponge, I always try to absorb information. I'm not the type of coach that says, no, no, I've been doing this forever and I'm going to keep on doing this. No, I always try to change. I always try to add more knowledge to my experience and try to be a better coach every year. So this is what I've been trying to do and I think the philosophy that I call mini players shows that I have to be concerned about how can I improve these little skills from this little kid to make them better for the next stage. I'm not going too fast, not trying to reach a big goal and jumping on stages or phases. I have to go very, very slow, very slow. I want them to understand in order to reach a goal, you have to follow little, little steps and try to conquer different goals and then we can move on.

Yeah, that is a wonderful philosophy. You explained also throughout the presentation, the power of teaching with progressions and that was very evident once the kids got to orange stage. Where does a coach find this methodology and if they aren't getting it from their mentor coach, where can they sort of find this and how did you learn this? Well, I'm curious and probably this is funny, but I've never been a player. I've never competed. I've never been in a tennis program. So in the back of my head, I see a kid and I say, okay, when I was his age or her age, I didn't know how to do this, so I have to do it by myself. So I'm going to help these kids to reach this, to be able to hit better shots, use better footwork to get in proper position. I'm always trying to, I feel like a doctor, I'm trying to give them remedy for certain problems they have and try to improve them little by little, but not going too fast. That's my philosophy. Yeah, I guess just to further that though, when you teach in progressions, that's a really skillful art and you're also layering in that tactical foundation as well throughout. So teaching them where to stand, where to follow through, sorry, where to go to when they're going to the net, covering the line, all those sort of skills that it's not just stationary, is it? Well, the thing is, I see sometimes that we as coaches make mistakes by thinking, okay, if I, for example, I feed balls to these kids for him, and I want him to hit more topspin.

And I always, I will always say, okay, tip of the racket, moving up, up, up, spin the ball, brush the ball, probably because we're saying this, we think, okay, the kid's going to understand it and it's going to reproduce it. And that's not the way it works. When a kid does not know how to do something, you can say it probably a thousand times, but the kid's not going to do it. So what do you do? What I do is, I do progressions, I make him feel something, make him, I use, sometimes it's my imagination, sometimes I have tools that allow me to get to those goals. But I try to make him understand what they need to do in order to improve a forehand, a topspin forehand, for example, or the way I have to hit a slice back in, a shot that I love. And all my girls, I have a team, an under 10 team that I'm coaching right now that I love it. And they always, from the very first week, they started hitting slice backings, because we lose a lot of progressions on the continent of it. So they all know that. And they know that most of the girls that are playing against, they don't know how to hit that shot. And they feel, you know, they feel better. They have more confidence because they see that they do some stuff that other players are not doing. Yeah, and it's so wonderful that you've recognized that because we're seeing slice is just really, really coming back strong. We'll never really left tennis, to be honest, with Ash Barty and Dan Evans and these players that really

Talk to us a little bit about that. Number one, if you think about the continental grip is the grip value you use for most, most shots. So what I do is just a warm up, for example, for these girls under 10 or for orange ball kids. What I do is they, they start very close to each other and that they just hit the balls. And they start doing mini runs, even with no nets, using continental grip, if they have the whole the racket from the top of the grip, they do that in order to get used to the grip. So by the time I try to teach them how to do volleys, how to do a slice back end or how to pronate to have better serve, they've been used to that. So they've been practicing the grip so it's not something new. I don't quite like kids serving with the forehand grip, because I know most coaches say yeah but this is a good way to have the kids serving from the very beginning. The problem is, if you have a seven year old kid playing with a forehand grip and a serve, that kid is now 10. So why are you going to stop, stop the kid, teach the continental grip, and the kids are playing competitions and say no, no, no, we have a tournament now, we can't change the grip now, because I'm not going to serve properly, or my kids not going to serve properly, or my play is not going to do it.

One of the girls is also playing basketball. So she's coming once a week for two hours. But the rest of the team, they're playing Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays for two hours. Okay. Other groups in the program have one hour and a half of tennis and half hour of physical training. What I do with them is they don't do physical training. They stay in my session for two hours. But since we work a lot on footwork, stability, the dynamics of the session, they're very physical in terms of not lifting weights. I'm talking about the way they have to move, they have control the body, they control the balance. I keep them for two hours on the court.

And what I try to do with them is we don't, I don't really like them to play every weekend. Because we are near Barcelona. Barcelona is a place where you can play tournaments Saturday and Sunday, the entire year. And some kids, the problem they have is get burned out by playing so many tournaments. And when they're 14, they have more tournaments than Ivan Lendo. Yeah. Yeah. Trying to get that balance of match play and development. And really, really what we're talking about is the concept of early specialization. And the other thing is, first of all, I like them to play team competitions is the way that I think the proper way to introduce kids into competition. And second, when I'm in a club, I talk to other coaches nearby, I can say, listen, I have four girls this age, I have three boys this age. How about if you come on Saturday with some kids, I'd send you video so you can see the level of them. And we play friendly matches. Yeah, so really getting that social aspect as well. So I take, make conclusions out of what is what I see in those friendly matches. And obviously they play individual singles tournaments, but I don't like heavy schedules. I don't like that they need to understand how to play they need to really get to know how to play the game.
